story: Oduduwa was a divine king and progenitor figure who came from the village of Oke Ora and became holder of the title of ruler of Ile-Ife, the Yoruba holy city. He served as progenitor of many independent royal dynasties among the Yoruba. Tradition holds that Oduduwa and his group disrupted the political structure of thirteen communities led by Obatala, causing conflict across several generations until a great smallpox outbreak forced a truce, uniting the communities into a single state under Oduduwa. Some of the opposing faction left to found new communities near the coast, while others stayed to continue the conflict. Later, Oranyan, son of Ogun and youngest grandson of Oduduwa, was the most warlike of the princes. The city suffered raids from remnants of the opposing faction, but Oranyan learned their secrets from Moremi and ended the raids, bringing lasting peace with her help. Oranyan spread the model of kingship through his own offspring, establishing dynasties in two prominent kingdoms, then returned home to claim the crown of Oduduwa. Up to sixteen princes left the city to found their own kingdoms, all remembered as descendants of Oduduwa, who is still revered as ancestor by the Yoruba people. In the creation tradition, Oduduwa was sent from heaven by the supreme god Olodumare to create the earth upon the waters, a mission taken from the sibling-consort Obatala, who had been given a snail shell filled with sand and a rooster to scatter it. Oduduwa is symbolized as the bottom half of a calabash, Obatala as the top. In another story, Obatala discovered the secret of his wife Oduduwa and stole her masquerade robes to wear himself. A separate, non-Yoruba tradition claims Oduduwa was son of Damerudu (also called Lamurudu), son of a magician king named Kisra, who fought in a great battle against a religious leader, lost, and migrated from Arabia into Africa, founding many kingdoms and dynasties along the way.
